- Here are my thoughts:
- 
- What first attracted you about the project?

In 2015 I started to publish open source code, after years of using it, I wanted to contribute back to the open source community. Open source code is how we can distribute good practices and stable infrastructure, It’s the way technology evolve in today’s society. From all friends at the BSD community that work on the open source code that is the base layer for apple, netflix and other giant tech consumer providers that we use in our day to day life. I believe working on Open Source code is one of the most important things there is. So I love open source that was one main part of how I got here, the next part is Substrate. Me and a friend of mine was the first rust developers on a newer chain(known today as picasso). This led me deeper into substrate, after jumping overboard from that ship, I wanted to continue working with substrate, I have accumulated this knowledge and experience in substrate and after spending time with **dwulf**(hat’s off to douglas) he showed me the vision Gavin Wood has behind I was totally sold. I was aware of Edgeware very loosely, after doing more research I found out that Edgeware was this stable pillar in the substrate ecosystem. But what really attracted me to the project was that Edgeware is a DAO. Not just marketing pitches and fancy words, but the front runner and a prime example of a community owned project. Edgeware unlike other blockchain’s is not a smaller tech team that is some division of a midsize VC company that is just spitting money left and right. As a developer/programmer/penetration tester/basically all roles that makes you spend large amount of time developing a new feature, reversing a binary, manipulating input, building things, time consuming things that you fail and fail at and then you make it work and you brain gets filled with dopamine and endorphins and you feel great.  The substrate community is very friendly so getting help from other developers working on other chains is always possible which is amazing. I also participated in some community quizzes and they went pretty well for me (2nd rank - thanks Gagan for all the fun). You can also call me David as it's how non-machine individuals are used to calling me btw.

I'm currently researching in blockchain governance/publications platforms which are, to me, the first block that needs to be implemented in the ecosystem to build the next cutting-edge applications for a better world. This way, I feel very close to the cypherpunk ideology. I have also been reading about libertarianism for years so I deeply think that both liberty and equality are needed at the same time to litteraly change the world based on shared values through the network effect, for which blockchain technologies can be very useful. As for it, EDG immediately seemed like a good place to debate and iterate on this field as an even more chaotic playground than Kusama already is.

I also have a background in eth DeFi (derivatives options),  web2 fintechs (micro-credit) and my original formation are on product management (mainly in the AI field) & entrepreneurship (top10 BS in Europe - FT ranking). I like to design products, make up development strategies, and manage all kinds of different systems to help fixing broken things in society. My interests in science, economy, philosophy, and politics make me always try to get the big picture when building something, which I think is the right path to creating long-term and systemic changes in our world.

But let's talk about what Edgeware is to me. 

> _What first attracted you about the project?_
> _What problems do you see Edgeware addressing?_

To me, there is no better definition than a Network for Edgeware. Simple but true.

To follow the last trend initiated by Vitalik on Balaji's concept, in my opinion, Edgeware truly has the potential for becoming a Network State, as a decentralized system based on shared values. Moreover, these values are promoting equality, so they can solve our societies' main issues of inequality and eventually eradicate poverty in a broader sense.

The thing I found the most interesting in the EDG ecosystem was the idea of Public Networks, like Common Good Parachains which really got me into DotSama (hello RMRK). This idea of evolving into a grass-root incubator for DotSama common-good-oriented parachains is brilliant as well, and I really look forward to seeing Kabocha coming alive, and seeing EDG as a relay chain, both onboarding the next DotSama parachains in their own way.

I also found the EDG spirit very amazing. Everyone is so kind and helpful, very proactive, and philosophically aligned. I've not been here for a long time but I guess it doesn't mean there are no drama and heated debates, but as long as everyone is respectful and knows when to put their ego aside, it's always benefiting everyone. I am French so I am pretty used to these kinds of living debates, from which I certainly know that they always benefit us all.

> _What is Edgeware not for?_

This question is very important to me as it really defines where we are going as a community, so I will make it very simple:

Edgeware is not for building on-chain casinos, onboarding web2 centralized companies, or looking for institutional parties to help us scale.

We are a consensus made of values, and this is how we can host a network effect. Plus, thanks to Substrate, our tech is amazing so we can focus on what really matters to us: sharing our values by developing great products.

> _What other projects do you follow or think Edgeware could improve upon?_
> _What lessons do you think Edgeware can learn from other projects?_

I don't think there are many existing projects that Edgeware could improve upon, mainly because we are still very early in the concept of Network Publics or Network Services. I think staying underground in our eco and building things from scratch would better benefit us, because we would already have a consensus-made basis of users and platforms relying on state-of-the-art technologies.

I actually think the general DotSama eco should be more aware of Edgeware and participate more in our debates and I hope Kabocha will bring this awareness while incubating the next cutting-edge parachains.

> _What founding values or principles do you think Edgeware should have?_

To me, Edgeware should definitely be inspired by Libertarianism values. 

To quote Wikipedia:

> Libertarianism originated as a form of left-wing politics such as anti-authoritarian and anti-state socialists like anarchists, especially social anarchists, but more generally libertarian communists/Marxists and libertarian socialists. These libertarians seek to abolish capitalism and private ownership of the means of production, or else to restrict their purview or effects to usufruct property norms, in favor of common or cooperative ownership and management, viewing private property as a barrier to freedom and liberty. Left-libertarian ideologies include anarchist schools of thought, alongside many other anti-paternalist and New Left schools of thought centered around economic egalitarianism as well as geolibertarianism, green politics, market-oriented left-libertarianism, and the Steiner–Vallentyne school.

I think Edgeware totally understands the political issues that blockchain can raise when economic incentives are too rewarded. We need to keep this in mind to include as many people as possible in this debate, and to bring awareness to the whole crypto world about these risks and limitations. 

By the way, I am currently thinking of writing something about this on Polkassembly to promote Edgeware to Kusama as a political statement. If anyone wants to help, feel free to reach out!

> _What areas in the wider crypto-sphere interest you?_

Metaverse, NFTs, DeFi, I'm curious about everything, as long as it has been built for a better world.

> _What areas or communities outside of crypto interest you?_

Aside from my interests in many different areas, I've been DJing and producing electronic music for several years, you can check my Soundcloud profile here: [https://soundcloud.com/davyjonesmusic](https://soundcloud.com/davyjonesmusic). My productions are not made for clubs so I don't play them when I DJ (I prefer mixing Disco :) ) but it's my own way of expressing myself so I keep doing both in my own way.

By the way, I am also working with some friends in Paris on a side project for Kabocha, including exclusive physical parties and metaverses retransmission. It's also why I'm very excited about Kabocha as my creative part missed a chaotic playground to experiment with artistic stuff.

> _What does success look like to you? (what kind of a world do you see?)_

I would be satisfied if I could access a digital world allowing both transparency and privacy depending on my own will, where both liberty and equality would be constantly promoted, which means open-sourced and permissionless. I know this is not a one-man's job but if we succeed, I would consider I succeeded.

> What does failure look like to you?

To me, failure is this feeling of frustration not being able to assess in real life what my expectations of a product I am building is actually delivering. It also requires to regularly let down my ego in order to fully understand a user's expectations and to deliver what people are actually waiting for instead of what I initially had in mind.

Thank you again for this written exercise Rich, I would also love to read your answers to these questions!
